characters.name: Nahum

genealogy.note: Scripture gives no genealogy for Nahum — only his gentilic 'the Elkoshite' (Nahum 1:1), identifying him by hometown rather than lineage. Elkosh's location is not stated anywhere else in Scripture and remains disputed (proposed sites include a Galilean village, a town in/near Assyria, and Capernaum — literally 'village of Nahum' — none confirmed by the text itself).

verses.note: "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite." The only verse in the book that names him; everything else is his oracle, spoken but never narrated as biography.

"Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!" Nahum's own herald-imagery for the announcement his prophecy makes to Judah, almost identical to Isaiah 52:7.

funFacts: Nahum's name (Hebrew Nachum) means 'comfort' or 'consoler' — fitting, since his entire message functions as comfort for Judah, delivered by pronouncing the downfall of Judah's oppressor Nineveh.

NAMING COLLISION: KJV Luke 3:25 lists 'Naum' — the same underlying name rendered differently by the KJV translators — as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy through Heli/Mary. This Naum has no stated connection whatsoever to Nahum the prophet; the text links them by name only, not by identity.

Nahum is one of only a few Minor Prophets whose entire book is a single continuous oracle against a foreign nation, with no call narrative, no oracle against Judah or Israel itself, and no biographical material beyond the one-verse superscription.
characters.perkNote: Represents the vision breaking through in one unbroken oracle — bonus reflects Nahum's role as the sole messenger who receives and proclaims the entire prophecy.

characters.name: Nineveh (the Burden of Nineveh)
characters.purpose: The book's central oracle: a formal doom-pronouncement ('burden') declaring Nineveh's total, final destruction as God's righteous judgment for the city's cruelty — explicitly recalling that Nineveh had 'afflicted' Judah (1:12) and describing Nineveh as a 'bloody city' full of 'lies and robbery' (3:1) that made merchandise of nations through 'whoredoms' and 'witchcrafts' (3:4). It teaches that the LORD is 'slow to anger' yet will 'not at all acquit the wicked' (1:3) — that no empire's cruelty escapes reckoning, however secure it appears. (Attribution: Nahum)

verses.note: The oracle's formal heading: "The burden of Nineveh."
"But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies." Source of this tier's flood imagery.
"...I will cut off the graven image and the molten image out of the house of thy gods... for thou art vile." Addressed to the king/gods of Assyria.
The siege breaks: "the gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved... Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: yet they shall flee away."
Nineveh mocked as an emptied lions' den: "Where is the dwelling of the lions...? I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts."

"Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery... because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms."
"...Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?"
Closing dirge addressed to 'the king of Assyria' (left unnamed by the text): "thy nobles shall dwell in the dust... there is no healing of thy bruise."

funFacts: The Hebrew word translated 'burden' (massa) is the standard term for a doom-oracle against a foreign nation elsewhere in the prophets (e.g. Isaiah 13-23) — Nahum's whole book is structured as one of these, aimed entirely outward at Nineveh rather than at Israel or Judah.

Nahum 2:7 KJV capitalizes 'Huzzab' as though it were a proper name ('Huzzab shall be led away captive'), and some readers have taken it as a queen or goddess figure — but the underlying Hebrew is genuinely disputed among translators (it can also be read as a verb, roughly 'it is decreed'). This index does not treat Huzzab as a confirmed named individual, since the text itself does not settle the question.

Nineveh had already repented once, generations earlier, under a prophet's preaching — in Jonah. Nahum's oracle assumes that reprieve has run out; the two books bracket Nineveh's mercy and its final judgment, though Nahum itself never states this connection explicitly.
characters.perkNote: Bonus represents the oracle's escalating certainty — scales with how thoroughly each chapter details Nineveh's fall, from the opening warning (ch.1) through the siege (ch.2) to the final dirge (ch.3).

characters.name: No (No-amon / Thebes)
characters.purpose: A historical precedent cited within the oracle against Nineveh: the real Egyptian city of No (No-amon, i.e. Thebes) fell to conquest and captivity despite being defended by rivers, a sea-like rampart, and the combined strength of Ethiopia and Egypt (3:8-9) — Nahum argues that if No could still fall, Nineveh's own defenses will not save it either ('Art thou better than populous No...', 3:8). (Attribution: Nahum)

verses.note: "Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?"
"Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers."

"Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains."

funFacts: No-amon is the ancient Egyptian city Thebes, called 'No' or 'No-amon' ('city of [the god] Amon') elsewhere in the KJV (compare Jeremiah 46:25, Ezekiel 30:14-16). Nahum 3:8 is the only place the KJV renders it simply 'No.'

Ethiopia, Egypt, Put, and Lubim (3:9) are named here as nations/allies supplying No's strength, not individuals — none receive personal character treatment in Nahum; the text uses them only to establish how formidable No's defenses had been before its fall.
characters.perkNote: A smaller passive bonus than the Nineveh tier, themed as proof-by-precedent — supporting evidence within Nahum's argument rather than the book's main subject.

notes: SELF-CHECK: (1) Naming collision explicitly flagged per the fact-check note — KJV Luke 3:25 lists "Naum" (same underlying name as "Nahum") as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy through Heli/Mary; this Naum is unrelated to Nahum the prophet and the collision is documented in Nahum's funFacts. (2) No intra-book naming collisions found — Nahum contains only one named human individual (the prophet himself); "No," "Nineveh," "Elkoshite," "Ethiopia," "Egypt," "Put," and "Lubim" are all place/nation names, not competing personal names. (3) KJV-exact spelling verified against the text: "Nahum," "Elkoshite," "Nineveh," "No," "Huzzab," "Put," "Lubim." (4) "Huzzab" (2:7) was deliberately NOT given a character entry — KJV capitalizes it as a proper name, but the underlying Hebrew is genuinely disputed (it may be a verb, not a name), so treating it as a confirmed individual would risk asserting something the text doesn't clearly say; the ambiguity itself is documented instead. (5) Roster is intentionally thin (one person-tier, two law-tiers) because Nahum is only 3 chapters/47 verses and is structured as a single continuous oracle against Nineveh with essentially no other named individuals — this reflects the book's actual content, not incomplete indexing. (6) Schema hygiene: every managerId/parentManagerId referenced (nahum, nineveh, no_thebes) has a full matching characters[] entry; all parentManagerId values are null since there are no submanagers in this book; law entries (nineveh, no_thebes) omit "genealogy" entirely per methodology and instead carry "deliveredBy"/"purpose," while still retaining ageEvents/verses/funFacts/perkFlavor/perkNote for field consistency with the person entry; genealogyLists was omitted as unused (Nahum contains no bulk lists of named individuals, only nation names, which are cited in funFacts/purpose instead).
